conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a clinician who works with new mothers on the emotional ups and downs that can come after a baby arrives. I’m so glad you’re here today.

I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes doing a quick check-in called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s a simple, 10-question tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past week. There’s no pass or fail—just honest answers that will guide us in figuring out what kind of support might be most helpful for you right now.

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the small team directly involved in your care. You can take your time, and if any question feels hard to talk about, we can pause or come back to it.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt pretty difficult?

I’ve still laughed a little—mostly when my husband makes silly faces at the baby—but it’s not like before. A lot of times I feel too tired or foggy to really find things funny, even when I know they’re supposed to be.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I wouldn’t say “yes, all the time.” It’s more like “sometimes.” I can still laugh here and there, but it feels muted—like I have to remind myself to enjoy the moment instead of it just happening naturally.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—grabbing coffee with a friend, even just a quiet shower—but now it feels like I’m just getting through the day. I’ll think “that could be nice,” but the spark isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. Like when the baby wouldn’t settle and I kept thinking maybe I’m not feeding him right or I missed some cue. My head tells me it’s not my fault, but in the moment I still catch myself wondering what I did wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, that happens. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly my heart’s racing—what if he stops breathing, what if I’m not making enough milk, what if I’m doing everything wrong? There’s no real trigger; it just bubbles up and sits in my chest until I distract myself.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes. It’s not like a full panic attack, but I’ll get this sudden tightness in my chest—like something bad is about to happen—even when the baby’s fine and the house is quiet. It passes pretty quickly, maybe a couple of times a week.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, quite often. Between feedings, diapers, trying to sleep, and just keeping us both alive, it feels like there’s no room to breathe. Some days I end up crying in the shower because it all piles up and I can’t see it getting easier.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

A few nights this week I couldn’t fall asleep even when the baby was out. My mind just keeps ticking—going over everything I might’ve messed up or worrying something will happen to him. I’d lie there for an hour or two before finally drifting off, then wake up at the slightest sound.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah, I do feel that way some days—not every moment, but it hits in waves. Like yesterday afternoon everything just felt heavy and gray for a couple of hours, even though nothing bad had happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really. I’ve teared up a couple of times—once when I couldn’t get the baby to latch and another time when my mom left after visiting—but I haven’t had that full-on, can’t-stop sobbing kind of crying.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself. My baby needs me, and that’s not something I’d ever consider.

You've shared that the joy and spark you used to feel have been replaced by a muted, heavy mood that comes in waves. Even when you can laugh, it feels forced, and simple pleasures like a quiet shower now feel flat. You're sleeping poorly because your mind races with worries about doing motherhood "right," and you often blame yourself when things don't go perfectly, even though you rationally know it isn't your fault. Several times a week your chest tightens with sudden dread, and you're crying in the shower because the day-to-day feels overwhelming. Despite this, you remain firmly devoted to your baby and have no thoughts of harming yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Laughing only "sometimes" and feeling "muted" maps to "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports marked loss of anticipatory joy, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame "a few times this week" and describes it occurring during specific caregiving situations, aligning semantically with "Yes, some of the time".</sym>, <sym>Spontaneous, intrusive, recurrent worries without external triggers occur "very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes episodic chest tightness and dread without trigger, occurring "sometimes" and "a couple of times a week," aligning with "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>"Yes, sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes several nights of difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing thoughts, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports episodic sadness that recurs "some days" and lasts for hours, indicating a frequent pattern consistent with "Yes, quite often" option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Eight of the 10 EPDS items score 2 or 3, giving a total of 18. This exceeds the ≥14 threshold for probable <med>postpartum depression</med>. Key symptoms map to <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: diminished interest/pleasure (<quote>the spark isn't there</quote>), depressed mood (<quote>heavy and gray</quote>), guilt/worthlessness, anxiety/panic episodes, and insomnia. There is no self-harm ideation, so acute safety risk is absent, yet functional impairment is evident. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>PCP</med> or perinatal psychiatrist for full diagnostic evaluation
2. Discuss evidence-based treatments (CBT, IPT, sertraline) compatible with breastfeeding
3. Support <sym>sleep hygiene</sym> strategies and enlist partner/family for one longer stretch of rest
4. Provide 24-h crisis line numbers and schedule re-screen in 1-2 weeks
5. Offer referral to local new-parent support group and home-visiting nurse if available
6. Encourage partner or trusted adult to attend next visit to help implement plan
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Screening Summary – Postpartum Visit

Symptoms/Concerns
- Anhedonia: diminished capacity for pleasure/enthusiasm (Q1, Q2)
- Excessive guilt/self-blame (Q3)
- Persistent, non-triggered anxiety and episodic chest tightness/panic (Q4, Q5)
- Frequent sense of being overwhelmed, tearfulness (Q6)
- Mood-congruent insomnia (Q7)
- Intermittent sad/miserable mood with tearful spells (Q8, Q9)

Patterns
- Symptoms present "quite often" or "a few times/week", beginning post-delivery
- No self-harm ideation (Q10)

Screening Significance
Findings consistent with probable postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety. Highest endorsed areas: enjoyment loss, anxiety/panic, sleep disruption, coping difficulties.

Risk Factors
- Depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt, anxiety/panic, sleep problems, crying spells
- Denies suicidal or infanticidal thoughts; no self-harm intent → no acute safety alert at this time

Observation
Client endorses multiple depressive and anxious symptoms of clinical concern; recommends formal diagnostic evaluation and discussion of supports/interventions.
